content_voiceover: Large granular lymphocyte leukemia represents clonal proliferation of either cytotoxic T cells or NK cells, and distinguishing the two subtypes by immunophenotype and clonality studies is a classic board question. T-LGL leukemia arises from activated cytotoxic T cells, phenotypically CD3 positive, CD8 positive, CD57 positive, and or CD16 positive, frequently with loss of CD5 and CD7, and importantly it does show clonal TCR gene rearrangement, confirming its T cell origin. NK-LGL leukemia, by contrast, arises from NK cells, phenotypically CD3 negative, CD8 positive, CD16 positive, and or CD16 and CD56 positive, frequently losing CD2 and CD7, and it lacks TCR clonal rearrangement since NK cells don't rearrange their T cell receptor genes; it often shows abnormal killer immunoglobulin-like receptor, or KIR, expression instead, which serves as a surrogate marker of clonality. Clinically, both subtypes present with neutropenia and anemia, and there's a well known association with rheumatoid arthritis, sometimes referred to as Felty-like syndrome when neutropenia, splenomegaly, and RA coexist. There is no standard therapy, and the disease typically follows an indolent course, so treatment is reserved for symptomatic or cytopenic patients rather than given routinely.
keypoints: NK-LGL: CD3-/CD8+/CD16+/CD56+, no TCR rearrangement, often abnormal KIR expression
Clinical triad: neutropenia, anemia, and association with rheumatoid arthritis
No standard therapy; generally indolent course
keypoint_voiceover: Remember the key discriminator: T-LGL is CD3 positive with clonal TCR rearrangement, while NK-LGL is CD3 negative, lacks TCR rearrangement, and instead shows abnormal KIR expression. Both present with cytopenias and a notable rheumatoid arthritis association, and both typically follow an indolent course without a single standard treatment.
